newsitem.title: UK: Full text of January 15 UK monetary minutes.
newsitem.headline: Full text of January 15 UK monetary minutes.

text.p: The following is the complete text of the minutes of the January 15 monthly monetary policy meeting between Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke and Bank of England Governor Eddie George.
The Chancellor of the Exchequer and the Governor of the Bank of England met, together with officials, on January 15, to review monetary developments.
Monetary and Economic Developments

2. Latest monetary and economic data (reviewed by officials before the meeting) provided further evidence that cost pressures remained weak, and the exchange rate continued to strengthen. However, there were continuing signs that activity growth remained strong, although more forward-looking indicators of business confidence and consumer demand were less buoyant.
Inflation Indicators
3. Underlying inflation (RPI excluding mortgage interest payments - RPIX) was unchanged in November, at 3.3 per cent. All-items RPI inflation was also unchanged, at 2.7 per cent.
4. Most other indicators confirmed that cost pressures remained weak:
-- sterling non-oil commodity prices were little changed in November. However, the oil price had fallen back slightly to $23.4 per barrel;
-- sterling's effective exchange rate index had continued to rise sharply from 93.1 before the last meeting, to 96.0 currently;

-- total non-oil import prices fell by 1.0 per cent in the three months to October compared to the previous three months, and were 2.0 per cent lower than a year ago. Non-EU import prices fell by 1.9 per cent in the three months to November on the previous three months;

-- producer input prices for manufacturing (excluding food, beverage, tobacco and petroleum industries) fell in December by 0.9 per cent; and compared to a year ago they were 7.9 per cent lower. The CIPS survey input price indicator also fell again in December;

-- producer output prices (excluding FBTP) rose by 0.1 per cent in December; and the annual inflation rate was unchanged at 0.8 per cent. The CBI survey output price expectations balance rose in December;

-- the annual growth rate of underlying average earnings was unchanged in November, at 4.0 per cent for the fifth successive month;and IRS median pay settlements were also unchanged at 3.0 per cent in November.
Monetary and Financial Indicators
5. Notes and coin grew by 0.6 per cent in December, down from 0.7 per cent in November; and the annual growth rate fell slightly, to 7.2 per cent. M0's annual growth rate fell to 7.0 per cent.
6. M4 grew by 1.1 per cent in November, up from 0.8 per cent in October. The annual growth rate of M4 and M4 lending rose, to 10.3 per cent, and 9.5 per cent, respectively.

7. The Halifax house price index rose by 1.2 per cent in December, and the annual rate rose to 8.4 per cent . The Nationwide index fell by 0.3 per cent in December, although it was 8.5 per cent up on a year earlier. Housing market transactions continued to grow strongly; in the three months to November particulars delivered (which lag actual transactions) were 11.6 per cent up on the previous three months, and 24.9 per cent higher than a year earlier.

8. Short-term interest rates had risen slightly in the US and Japan since the last meeting, but had fallen by around 10 basis points in Germany. UK short-term interest rates were slightly higher on a month ago; forward rates implicit in short-sterling futures contracts had fallen (by less than 10 basis points) at all maturities, although they had risen by up to 20 basis points during the period before falling back again.

9. After rising initially 10-year bond yields ended up little changed in Germany and Japan, but had risen by over 30 basis points in the US. In the UK, yields on conventional gilts had also risen initially, but subsequently fell back, ending up less than 10 basis points higher at all maturities. Since the last meeting inflation expectations impliedby the gilt yield curve (calculated by the Bank from the difference between the yields on conventional and index-linked bonds) were little changed for 5 years ahead, but hadrisen by nearly 10 basis points for 10 years ahead.
Activity Indicators

10. In the US recent data confirmed that output was growing at around trend. However, employment grew more strongly than expected in December, although unemployment was unchanged at 5.3 per cent. Industrial production rose by 0.9 per cent in November, following a fall of 0.2 per cent in October. In Japan industrial productionfell by 0.2 per cent in November, following a rise of 3.9 per cent in October.

11. In Germany GDP grew by 0.8 per cent in Q3. Growth was almostexclusively from exports and domestic demand remained weak. Industrial production rose by 1.6 per cent in November, reversing falls over the previous two months. Retail sales fell by 3.9 per cent in October, and the November survey of retail confidence showed continuing weakness. In France GDP grew by 0.9 per cent in Q3, following a fall of 0.2 percent in Q2. Industrial production fell by 0.8 per cent in October, following a fall of 1.4 per cent in September. Unemployment rose slightly in November, to 12.7 per cent.

12. The latest estimates of UK GDP growth in Q3 showed that both whole economy and non-oil GDP grew by 0.7 per cent, and were respectively 2.4 per cent and 2.3 per cent higher than a year earlier. Consumer spending rose by 1.0 per cent in Q3, leaving it 3.2 per cent up on a year earlier. Investment overall fell by 2.0 per cent in Q3,but it was 3.3 per cent higher than a year earlier.
13. Most other activity data were consistent with output growth continuing above trend, although indicators of business confidence and consumer demand were less buoyant:

-- manufacturing output fell by 0.5 per cent in November, but in the three months to November it was up 0.3 per cent on a year earlier. Total industrial output rose by 0.4 per cent in November, and in the latest three months was up 1.0 per cent on a year earlier;
-- most major business surveys continued to suggest continuingstrong growth in

activity, although at a slower rate than in previous months. The December CIPS and CBI surveys both showed a fall in output and new orders indicators, but they remained well above historical averages;

-- retail sales volumes rose by 0.7 per cent in November, following a rise of 0.4 per cent in October; and in the three months to November sales were 3.9 per cent higher than in the same period a year earlier;
-- but latest survey indicators in the retail sector had come off their peaks: consumer confidence fell in December, but remained at a high levelby historical standards;

-- the December CBI Distributive Trades Survey showed a sharp fall in the balance of retailers expecting higher sales (although the balanceremained strongly positive); and the December BRC survey showed continuing sales growth although at a slower rate;

-- claimant unemployment fell by 45,100 in December, followinga fall of 95,400 in November (although the fall was exaggerated by the introduction of the Job Seekers Allowance). The Autumn Labour Force Survey showed a much smaller fall in unemployment (down 32,000 in the quarter), although employment rose by 130,000, virtually all full-timers. Unfilled vacancies at Jobcentres fell by 1,200 in December.
Summary of discussion

14. The Governor said that, taken overall, developments since theDecember meeting did not substantially alter the monetary and economic picture as the Bank saw it then. The consumer-led expansion of domestic demand remained intact; and despite the further strengthening of the exchange rate and the lack of any immediate inflationary pressure at the producer stage, the Bank continued to think that this would put the inflation target increasingly at risk in the course of next year.

15. Looking, first, at demand and output, the revisions to the National Accounts to Q3, that had become available since the last meeting did not help to reconcile the substantial divergence between the income and output estimates on the one handand the expenditure estimates on the other. Nevertheless, it did seem clear that realpersonal disposable income had been growing strongly (by 4.6 per cent Q3 1996 on Q3 1995 - the largest annual increase since 1989 Q1) and that this had fed through into consumer spending (3.2 per cent up over the same period). And the signs were that this had continued in Q4. RPDI would have benefited from increasing employment (200,000 higher in Q3 - the largest increase since Q1 1989). Consumption looked to have increased quickly again in Q4. Retail sales volumes had risen by 0.4 per cent in October and 0.7 per cent in November; and despite some mixed anecdotal and survey evidence it seemed that December, too, had been reasonably, if not outstandingly, strong. Both narrow money growth (notes and coin rose at an annualised rate of 7.2 per cent in Q4); and the continued rapid growth of consumer borrowing (up 18.4 per cent in the three months to November at an annual rate) were consistent with consumption continuing to expand at an annual rate of 4 per cent or more, which was above the sustainable rate.

16. At the same time, the recovery in the housing market continued apace. The Halifax house price index had risen by 1.2 per cent in December, bringing the rise over the year to 8.4 per cent. Indicators of turnover and mortgage lending also continued to trend upwards (on the data to November) and house building activity continued to increase quite strongly (also to November).

17. The Governor said that, given the underlying strength of the household sector, while services sector output (which accounted for 63 per cent of total GDP) continued to grow above trend, at an average annual quarterly rate of around 0.8 percent, both total industrial production (28 per cent of GDP) and manufacturing output (23 per cent of GDP) were not as strong overall as might have been expected and remained erratic month by month. In the case of manufacturing there clearly were now concerns, in the surveys, of a prospective weakening of demand associated with the stronger exchange rate; but it was not clear from the external trade data (to October and November) that this had yet affected actual output. So that probably did not explain the surprising fall in manufacturingproduction in November, which had offset October's rise; but this was a noisy series.

18. Broad money growth had risen further since the Summer. M4 had increased by 1.1 per cent in November and was 10.8 per cent higher than a year before. Even making an allowance for the introduction of the gilt repo market and for some one-off transactions in November, the underlying 12-month rate of growth was around 9-1/2 percent and had been of this order now for over a year. As the Bank had said on a number of occasions before, that was very unlikely to be compatible with the inflation target in the medium term.

19. Turning to costs and prices, the Governor noted that there had been a small further fall in producer input prices in December, notwithstanding the recoveryin the oil price. This fall was clearly related to the further strengthening of sterling (up by 3.2 per cent on the ERI since the last meeting and by 14 per cent altogether since early August). Input prices overall had now fallen by nearly 6 per cent over the past year and by nearly 8per cent ex FBTP.

20. The tightening of the labour market had recently accelerated. The UK workforce in employment had increased by 200,000 in Q3, and GB employment had risen by 130,000 in the 3 months to November. Unemployment had fallen particularly sharply (by 95,000) in November and again in December (by 45,000). Although the Novemberunemployment figure in particular might have somewhat exaggerated the underlying fall, these data suggested an economy which was more buoyant than some of the official output data indicated. Even so they had not so far had much effect on labour costs: average earnings growth had again been unchanged, at 4 per cent, in both October and November, and pay settlements on average remained around 3-1/2 per cent. 21. Underlying manufacturing output prices remained very subdued; excluding FBTP they had risen only 0.1 per cent in December and were only 0.8 per cent above their level a year ago (as they had been in November).

22. The Governor said that retail prices nevertheless were still disappointing, with RPIX growing at 3.3 per cent in the year to November - unchanged from last month. A major influence in the past two months had been a strong rise in petrol prices, which had not been offset by reducing inflation of other goods, or of services.

23.The further strengthening of sterling since the December meeting meant that the Bank still expected RPIX inflation to moderate this year despite its recent resilience. The exchange rate appreciation would also have a longer-lasting effect throughits impact on net external demand. But the Bank did not expect this latter effect to be sufficient to offset stronger inflationary pressure re-emerging next year as a result of final domestic demand, particularly consumer demand, continuing to grow above trend; and the Bank still thought it was likely that a monetary tightening of 1/2 per cent would be needed fairly soon to moderate the growth of domestic demand. 24. There was a case for making a 1/2 per cent move now on the usual "stitch in time" basis. The Bank were not pressing that case at this point. There were still questions about some of the recent data, and, in terms of market tactics, a 1/2 per cent move this month could suggest that the authorities were more concerned about the gathering strength of domestic demand than was the case. But the Bank did strongly recommend a 1/4 per cent rise this month. If there were no move now, the Bank certainly would judge - and the market may well judge - the authorities were falling rather clearly behind the game and taking risks with the inflation objective. If, then, the upcoming data were to be relatively strong, expectations about the extent of the necessary rise in interest rates would escalate.

25. The Governor concluded that, with a 1/4 per cent rise now, it may well be, as the Bank had said last time, that a further 1/4 per cent rise would be needed if the data did confirm the strength of the economy. But that would depend upon the data, andmight involve less risk of an exaggerated reaction in financial markets. The Bank's clear advice was to raise rates now by 1/4 per cent.
26. The Chancellor said that the indicators published since the last meeting had been mixed. The evidence since last month had not become any clearer.

27. He recognised there were areas that needed to be kept a closeeye on. The housing market was recovering very strongly, albeit from a very weak base. Prices, and also activity, had picked up. Particulars delivered were up 25 per cent over thepast year, although they remained a long way below their previous peak. The building society house price indices were showing annual growth of around 8 per cent, but this came after a period from 1989 to 1995 when there had been no overall change in prices.

28. The money figures were also strong. Discounting the special factors relating to the gilt repo market, broad money was growing at over 9 per cent a year. But it had been growing at around this pace for around a year.

29. The Chancellor said he could see a case for raising interest rates taking the housing market and money supply figures in isolation, but other indicatorswere more mixed. Although consumption was still strong (and the December retail sales figures were not yet available), early indicators from the December CBI Distributive Trades Survey and the British Retail Consortium suggested that the rate of growth may have eased off somewhat.

30. The labour market figures, published that morning had been good. The Chancellor said that in his view the Labour Force Survey was the better guide to what was happening in the labour market. This showed unemployment falling and employment rising, but at a slower rate than the claimant count and the Workforce in Employment Survey. The Labour Force Survey showed a drop of only 32,000 in unemployment in the latest quarter. And the underlying downward trend in unemployment may be around 15-20,000 a month. The unemployment rate remained at 7.9 per cent on LFS data. The labour market was continuing to improve, but was not too tight yet. Earnings growth remained at 4 per cent without showing any sign of picking up, and manufacturing settlements remained at around 3 per cent.

31. The Chancellor said there were other indicators that argued against a rise in rates now. Manufacturing production had fallen by 1/2 per cent in November, reversing the rise in the previous month, and it was little changed on a year ago. Industrial production was only up 1 per cent on a year ago. The CBI industrial trends survey and the purchasing managers index suggested a marked slowdown in manufacturing activity. GDP growthhad been revised down to 0.7 per cent in the third quarter. Overall, the output indicators were fairly subdued.

32. The producer price data remained exceptionally good. Underlying output prices rose 0.8 per cent in the year to December, the lowest rate since the late 1960s. Underlying input prices fell by 7.9 per cent in the year to December compared to a fall of 7.1 per cent the previous month. Commodity prices were still falling and the oil price had eased. Cost pressures were not strong.

33. The Chancellor said he was not persuaded to put up interest rates given the strength of sterling. Sterling was now 7-1/2 per cent higher than when interest rates were last raised in October. It was 15 per cent higher in effective terms than when interest rates were cut a year ago, and 20 per cent higher against the deutschmark. Interest rate decisions were not dependent on the exchange rate, but it was one of the factors to be taken into account. The Chancellor said he did not believe that enough account had been taken of the strength of the exchange rate. Most economic models suggested an exchange rate change of this magnitude would have a significant effect on the prospects for inflation. The strength of the pound also would have a marked effect on activity, where the full effect had not been felt yet.

34. The Chancellor thought that much of the recent strength of the exchange rate was a reaction partly to the strength of the economy and partly to the expectation of higher interest rates, compared to other G7 countries. A modest 1/4 per cent rise in interest rates could stimulate further appreciation of sterling, by implying that ratescould go up further.
35. The current economic indicators were mixed, and in some respects conflicting. The stronger exchange rate was a disinflationary force which argued against an interest rate rise now.

36. The Governor agreed that the most recent data did not change the arguments significantly either way. But he was more concerned by the persistence of indicators of strong demand: the housing market was growing strongly; rapid growth of the moneysupply had persisted for over a year; the trend in consumer demand growth was still around 1 per cent a quarter (and even faster for spending on services); and the pace of tightening in the labour market was accelerating. He felt that in time the official output data were likely to be revised up. He recognised that the higher exchange rate posed a dilemma for policy; but it had been taken into account in the Bank's advice - it was a major reason why the Bank expected inflation to decline in 1997.
37. In discussion the following points were made:

-- while activity had strengthened recently, this was broadly in line with how the economy had been expected to develop. However, the risksfor the future were on the upside, especially for consumer demand - personal wealth had risen sharply, consumer credit was rising strongly, and households had still yet to benefit from building society windfalls. Unemployment was also continuing to fall, and consumer confidence remained high. This suggested consumer demand, which had grown by around 4 per cent over the last year, could accelerate further;

-- earnings growth had been stable for several months in theface of improving labour market conditions. Wages were still growing at a rate that was consistent with the inflation target; but if they picked up further,as had happened in previous upswings, this could put the target at risk;

-- the outlook for inflation in the short term was still good - it was likely to fall back towards 2-1/2 per cent during 1997 in response to very weak cost pressures. But inflation was currently above the target (although policy was based on the outlook for inflation, rather than the current rate); and it was higher than in many other European countries. Although many firms were adapting to a low-inflation environment, some of the indicators that had in the past given warning signals of a pick-up in inflation further ahead (in particular broadmoney and house prices) were rising strongly;

-- interest rates were now back to the level of last spring,although the economy had strengthened since then. A modest rise in interest ratesnow would still leave real rates relatively low by historical and international standards; and the rise in rates in response to the strengthening of demand would be very modest compared to previous cycles, either in the UK or abroad. However, the higher exchange rate (if it persisted) would be expected to have a direct effect on the domestic price level, as well as to reduce the growth of activity;

-- there were a number of factors underpinning the rise in sterling, including: dollar strength; market uncertainties about the prospects for EMU; the strength of the UK economy; and market expectations about the prospects for interest rates in the UK and overseas. It was important to take account of theexchange rate in setting policy; but on its own it would not rule out an interest rate rise if domestic conditions justified it (in the same way that it had not ruled out rate cuts when the exchange rate had been falling).
Conclusion

38. Summing up, the Chancellor said he had no intention of takingrisks with inflation. He would continue to set interest rates to achieve the inflation target, but he was not persuaded that an increase in rates was required this month. He had seriously considered the case for a 1/4 per cent rise in interest rates at the previous meeting, but haddecided against. The data published since had been mixed. Consumer demand was still growing strongly, but there was some suggestion in the early indicators for retail sales that the rate of growth had eased off slightly. The figures for industrial production, and manufacturingproduction in particular, were subdued, although the housing market and monetary growth remained strong. In addition, the exchange rate had strengthened again. He decided to leave interest rates unchanged in January.
